MO-IKE trains a dynamic retriever to optimize competing objectives in knowledge editing, enabling more balanced and globally coherent prompt construction. On Llama-3.2, MO-IKE improves edit success (reliability) from 85.0% to 92.0%, paraphrase consistency (generality) from 77% to 79%, while increasing retention rate (specificity) by 23.0% compared to prior RL-based methods.

authors.name: Xuzhong Wang, Maiqi Jiang, Tejal Nair, Girija Bhusal, Yanfu Zhang, Haipeng Chen

papers.title: AdaPath: Query-Adaptive Path-Finding via Path-Bank for Multi-Hop Implicit Biomedical KGQA
papers.summary: Path-finding over knowledge graphs has become an effective way to ground LLM reasoning on multi-hop questions. However, biomedical QA introduces two distinct challenges that general-domain methods are not designed for: (i) queries do not expose intermediate reasoning and can be answered through multiple valid pathways, and (ii) biomedical knowledge graphs are densely connected, so path-finding methods easily take wrong turns. To address these challenges, we propose AdaPath, a path-finding framework that retrieves query-adaptive meta-paths from Path-Bank, which captures both query semantics and biomedical knowledge graph structure. AdaPath provides the missing cues in biomedical queries while effectively pruning dense knowledge graph neighborhoods during multi-hop reasoning. We further release BioStrat-QA, a biomedical KGQA benchmark that stratifies multi-hop queries by how much intermediate reasoning they expose. Across biomedical KGQA benchmarks, AdaPath consistently outperforms baselines, sustaining meaningful path-finding even when multi-hop queries expose less surface information. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jun-Hyeong-Kim/AdaPath.

authors.name: Jun Hyeong Kim, Dongki Kim, Yinhua Piao, Sung Ju Hwang

papers.title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
papers.summary: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. We show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that they compare favorably to spending the extra compute on more audit attempts.

authors.name: Axel Ahlqvist, Richard Guan, Juan-Pablo Rivera, Adeline Kassler, Dmitrii Troitskii, Alexandra Souly, Kai Fronsdal, Robert Kirk, John Hughes

papers.title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents augmented by tools can automate complex, multi-step tasks, such as web navigation, code generation, and workflow orchestration, by acting on external systems through tool calls. However, hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations in LLMs, and the irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. These risks call for safeguards that can check requirements across a trajectory, both before actions execute and when recorded behavior is evaluated. We present ContrAgent, a contract-based framework for symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls and formalizes it as a trace over a fixed set of checkable predicates. It then specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTL$_f$). Each contract is compiled to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that serves two roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library, acting as a reusable knowledge base, is maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain. We show the effectiveness of our approach on four benchmarks spanning both roles, where ContrAgent is competitive with LLM-judge, classifier, and guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and, in the online mode, orders of magnitude lower per-call latency.

authors.name: Yifeng Xiao, Johnna Liu, Pierluigi Nuzzo

papers.title: Marginal utility, matrix factorization, and the Key-Value (KV) cache: a unified information-economic framework for sovereign geo-mining inference
papers.summary: This paper builds a theoretical bridge between the economic notion of marginal utility and two machine-learning constructs, matrix factorization and the Key--Value cache of transformer language models. The singular value spectrum of a rating matrix is shown to be a diminishing marginal utility schedule for latent factors, the eigenvalue spectrum of the projected covariance operator to be the marginal utility schedule of a model's learned representation, and cache eviction and low-rank cache compression to be instances of constrained utility maximization under a memory budget. The three collapse into a single allocation rule: retain the top dimensions whose eigenvalue exceeds the shadow price of the binding constraint. The framework is applied to the automated extraction of structured information from geo-mining documents, where it motivates a multi-pass inference protocol, a layer-wise TIES model merging procedure, and a selection policy combining extraction quality, localization drift and energy, scalarized with a Conditional Value-at-Risk term on drift. Two empirical contributions are reported. An 11.2-million-parameter hierarchical classifier, trained in about five minutes on a single GPU, reaches 90.0 per cent level-1 accuracy on a held-out test set from a 973-document uranium-exploration corpus, against 92.0 per cent for a proprietary model on a fifty-document human audit of the same corpus, at a latency of 2.62 ms per card against approximately 2,000 ms for the API and at negligible cost. A diagnostic of uniform-density TIES merging exposes a reproducible degenerate mode in which the merged model returns token-identical outputs across five geographically distinct districts while declaring high confidence; re-executing the merge under layer-wise calibrated densities removes that signature on the diagnostic sample. The full-scale extraction benchmark, including LoRA fine-tuning, is reported as projected rather than measured and remains an empirical extension of this work.

authors.name: Caroline Gans Combe (INSEEC)

papers.title: CaLR: Causal Latent Revision for Robust Diffusion Reasoning
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) models suffer from local greediness, while diffusion language models (DLMs) often lack the strict causal structure required for reasoning. To combine the advantages and overcome the drawbacks of the dual, we propose Causal Latent Revision (CaLR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as constrained latent optimization. By adopting a causal topology matrix (CTM) from an expert model and implicit differentiation, CaLR performs gradient-guided ``thought revision" to enforce logical consistency, enabling dynamic self-correction of intermediate steps during parallel generation. Empirically, CaLR achieves SOTA DLM performance on complex benchmarks, surpassing strong AR baselines and demonstrating superior robustness in constrained tasks like Sudoku.

authors.name: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li

papers.title: Finite-Sample Probabilistic Safety Certification for AI-Based Grid-Edge Coordination
papers.summary: Coordinating a large population of flexible grid-edge devices can alleviate the need for time-consuming and capital-intensive network upgrades. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based control methods such as multi-agent reinforcement learning or imitation learning are promising to this coordination due to their real-time decision scalability. However, system operators still need an independent and rigorous way to decide whether a given AI system is safe enough for deployment. This paper develops a \emph{finite-sample} probabilistic safety certification framework for AI-based grid-edge coordination. The central idea is to reduce the complete input--AI--decision--evaluation workflow to a binary unsafe outcome under an operator-defined safety specification, and then use exact binomial inference to certify the corresponding unsafe operation probability. Given a set of held-out calibration scenarios, the framework returns the tightest one-sided upper certificate and an accept/reject deployment criterion that controls the probability of false safety certification. Because the certification is for the calibration distribution that may \emph{deviate} from the future operation, we further combine the nominal certificate with physically interpretable sample-space adversarial attacks, a concept widely used in AI models to investigate their fragility. Case studies on grid-edge flexibility coordination with 1{,}000-agent AI models (independent parameters) verify the safety guarantee and the value of integrating adversarial attacks into a rolling-window training-certification-deployment flow.

authors.name: Yihong Zhou, Hanbin Yang, Thomas Morstyn

papers.title: Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion models have become leading architectures for inverse protein folding. Test-time alignment guides these models during inference to generate proteins with desirable attributes. Alignment methods for discrete diffusion models often treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking effective mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the masking structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of positions to edit by re-masking and re-sampling the corresponding tokens in a sequence. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pre-trained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models without modifying the underlying generative processes. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, Spectral Feedback increases the proportion of stable proteins by 32.3 percentage points over a pre-trained model, 24.8 over Best-of-10, and 5.8 over a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

authors.name: Shai Dickman, Mert Cemri, Landon Butler, Kannan Ramchandran

papers.title: GeoWind2Plan: Mission-Time 3D Urban Wind Prediction for Energy-Efficient UAV Planning
papers.summary: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, making unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) energy depend on local wind exposure as well as path length. However, building-resolved wind is rarely available when a mission must be planned. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) produces high-fidelity urban flow fields, but each simulation is tied to a fixed inflow boundary condition and can take hours to days, which is incompatible with urban UAV missions that typically last minutes to tens of minutes. We present GeoWind2Plan, a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework for mission-time 3D urban wind prediction and energy-efficient UAV planning. Given only a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan transforms the building geometry into a reference-wind frame, predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches with a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, stitches them into a local wind field, and optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. Rather than pursuing CFD-perfect reconstruction, GeoWind2Plan targets decision-useful wind prediction: trajectories are planned with predicted wind and evaluated under high-fidelity CFD wind. Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, GeoWind2Plan performs corridor-localized wind inference in about 3 s, compared with roughly 8 h for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time. Code/dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/GeoWind2Plan/ . Demo: https://geowind2plan.com .

authors.name: Shaoxiang Qin, Yucheng Zhao, Fuyuan Lyu, Di Zhou, Jiachen Yao, Xue Liu, Anima Anandkumar, Liangzhu Leon Wang, Xiongye Xiao

papers.title: Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination for Hospital Patient Flow Optimization
papers.summary: Efficient patient flow coordination across autonomous hospital departments is critical for mitigating overcrowding and balancing resource utilization. While classical queueing theory, specifically open Baskett--Chandy--Muntz--Palacios (BCMP) networks, provides an interpretable mathematical topology for healthcare operations, analytical models rely on stationary assumptions and fixed routing matrices that degrade under state-dependent real-world dynamics. Conversely, centralized reinforcement learning approaches struggle to accommodate the decentralized structure of hospital governance, where individual clinical departments function with localized observations, heterogeneous resources, and divergent operational objectives. In this paper, we present a Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) framework titled \emph{Physics-Informed Multi-Agent Coordination}, which embeds empirically calibrated BCMP queueing topologies as physical priors within a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning architecture. Formulated as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under coupled resource constraints, our method enables autonomous departmental agents to cooperatively negotiate patient routing and dynamic service scaling. To mitigate environmental non-stationarity without inducing excessive communication overhead, agents exchange localized action fingerprints along network edges and optimize a spatially decomposed reward structure. Empirical evaluations driven by real-world MIMIC-IV patient trajectories indicate that this cooperative multi-agent approach substantially reduces cumulative system delay compared to static Markovian approximations, heuristic dispatching, and independent multi-agent baselines, while maintaining clinical safety constraints.

authors.name: Guoqing Zhang, Rafik Hadfi, Takayuki Ito

papers.title: ReMem: Rethinking Perception and Memory in Long-Context Recommendation Agents
papers.summary: Recent Recommendation Agents (RecAgents) offer a promising alternative by shifting recommendation to an active, user-side paradigm, where generative agents autonomously perceive web platforms, reason over user preferences, and execute decisions. However, existing RecAgents still suffer from two critical limitations: brittle item perception based on noisy item pages, and inefficient long-context reasoning over extended user histories and multi-step interaction traces. To address these challenges, we propose a recommendation-agent framework, termed ReMem, that combines OCR-based multimodal perception with time-evolving dynamic memory. Instead of parsing raw HTML, ReMem observes item-page screenshots and uses an OCR tool to produce structured textual evidence for the reasoning backbone. To support long-horizon preference modeling, ReMem further introduces a chunk-wise sequential update strategy that maintains a bounded textual memory while processing histories longer than the backbone context window; with fixed chunk and memory budgets, the number of update calls grows linearly with history length. This design allows the agent to preserve evolving user preferences without relying on external memory modules or disrupting the standard autoregressive generation process. To train the dynamic memory updater, we further develop a multi-memory GRPO variant whose reward combines recommendation-specific information with final-task metrics. Experiments on three Amazon-derived datasets and a controlled post-retrieval protocol show an average relative improvement of 7.58% over the strongest reported baseline across searching, ranking, and judging tasks.

authors.name: Haohao Qu, Yongcheng Jing, Chun Hin Chan, Shanru Lin, Wenqi Fan, Dacheng Tao

papers.title: Alleviating Hallucination in Reasoning Tasks with Training-Free Uncertainty-Guided Steering
papers.summary: Recent work on hallucination detection in large language models has shown that, for a fixed pre-trained model and reasoning task, it is possible to estimate the model's confidence in the correctness of its outputs. Such uncertainty estimates have primarily been used to improve truthfulness by detecting or filtering confabulations. In this work, we ask whether these signals can instead be used more proactively to directly improve the accuracy of model-generated answers. We propose USteer, a simple, training-free steering mechanism that adjusts a model's layer-wise activations during inference using the gradient of a confidence measure with respect to the activations. This procedure nudges generation toward outputs with lower uncertainty at inference time, without modifying model parameters or requiring additional supervision. We show that this approach consistently reduces hallucination across a range of reasoning tasks, demonstrating that confidence signals can be leveraged not only for detection, but also for effective inference-time control of model behavior.

authors.name: Litian Liu, Qiqi Hou, Yubing Jian, Reza Pourreza, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Roland Memisevic, Yao Qin, Hong Cai

papers.title: What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?
papers.summary: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

authors.name: Keith J. Holyoak, Martin M. Monti

papers.title: LUMOS: Tracing Parametric Knowledge from Training Data to Behavioral Outputs in LLMs
papers.summary: Current analyses of LLMs' parametric knowledge are largely output-centric, drawing conclusions about what a model knows without verifying what it was actually trained on. This leaves fundamental questions, such as whether a correct response reflects genuine generalization or rote memorization, grounded in speculation rather than evidence. To resolve these ambiguities, we introduce LUMOS, a diagnostic framework that traces knowledge across training-data exposure, internal representations, and behavioral outputs, leveraging OLMo 2 with its fully transparent training corpus. By grounding analysis in verified exposure, we reveal that models internally encode rare facts with high separability (84%) yet fail to express them behaviorally (54%), though this retrieval gap narrows with scale. Furthermore, when models are asked to self-reflect on their own answers, they perform reliably on trained content (83%) but drop to random-baseline levels (49%) on unseen content. This collapse persists even under chain-of-thought prompting, which inflates confidence signals rather than improving calibration. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that incorporating the training-data axis into LLM evaluation transforms speculative diagnoses into verifiable claims, and we advocate that this axis should be a standard component of knowledge assessment in LLMs.

authors.name: Seoyeon Ye, Gayoung Kim, Jiyoung Hong, Sookyung Kim, Hyunsoo Cho

papers.title: ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching
papers.summary: Diffusion models for structured scientific generation must produce samples satisfying hard geometric constraints imposed by physics, chemistry, or biology, yet inference in these settings is prohibitively slow, demanding hundreds to thousands of neural-function evaluations per sample. We unify eight state-of-the-art models spanning medical volumetrics, molecular conformations, protein backbone design, crystal structure prediction, and multi-view 3D scenes under a single abstraction, Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), in which the target distribution is supported on a manifold defined by an externally specified constraint map. All existing acceleration families fail on this class: quantization exhausts memory on high-dimensional volumetric operators; pruning breaks constraint fidelity; fast ODE solvers allow trajectories to drift off the constraint manifold; and feature-caching heuristics are blind to constraint geometry, inducing mode confusion in the high-noise regime. We introduce ManifoldCache, the first training-free, data-free accelerator designed from first principles for CMDMs. The key insight is that the conditional score decomposes orthogonally into a normal component, which enforces constraint satisfaction, and a tangential component, which navigates within the manifold. Exploiting this structure, we prove that the noise-schedule midpoint is a sharp safe-caching boundary: caching before it incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a strictly positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion, a gap that persists up to the boundary. We further prove that deeper network blocks admit provably larger certified cache strides within the safe phase, as a consequence of the score decomposition propagating through block Jacobians. The resulting schedule requires no calibration data, along with zero training overhead.

authors.name: Prashant Pandey, Devineni Sri Venkatraya Chowdary, Brejesh Lall

papers.title: From Dialogue to Diagnostic Hypotheses: Evaluating LLM Agents for Psychiatric Assessment
papers.summary: Although LLMs show promising diagnostic reasoning on supplied clinical evidence, their ability to elicit such evidence through free-form psychiatric interviews remains less understood. We evaluate interview quality and diagnostic hypotheses using simulated patients and human participants. For controlled simulation, we introduce PsyCPG, transforming clinical cases into structured patient profiles. On 30 paired cases, experts rate PsyCPG simulations higher in quality than raw-case role-play (4.50 versus 3.83/5). We introduce PsyCIDRA, a dual-agent framework: its interviewer agent uses a notepad tool, expert-written skills, and ICD-11 reference tools to guide interviews; its diagnostic agent analyzes the transcript and produces a report for expert review, ranking differential diagnoses with supporting, conflicting, and missing evidence. Across four models and 53 development cases, PsyCIDRA achieves higher observed diagnostic agreement than direct prompting. On 81 held-out simulated cases, exact-code rank-1 accuracy reaches 60.5% versus 51.9%. We conduct 101 interviews with human participants; two psychologists, blinded to interview condition and model reports, independently assess interview quality and transcript-supported hypotheses. In separate arms, PsyCIDRA agrees with experts on whether to issue a hypothesis in 79.6% of cases versus 65.4% for direct prompting. This study provides an empirical basis for understanding and evaluating LLM agents in free-form psychiatric interviewing.

authors.name: Milad Mohammadi, Fatemeh Akrami Shamsabadi, Zahra Mohseni, Amirhossein Safdarian, Malekfarhad Malek, Hadi Moradi, Hesham Faili

papers.title: AssemState: Manual and Physical-State-Guided Reasoning for Zero-shot Furniture Assembly
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual understanding, but precise 3D spatial reasoning integrated with physical environment remains difficult. Furniture assembly requires not only recovering step-level operations from diagrammatic manuals, but also translating semantic attachment relations into 6D pose updates that enable parts to physically interact with the environment and previously assembled components. To study this problem, we propose AssemState, a zero-shot framework for manual and physical-state-guided furniture assembly. It firstly employs anchor-guided boundary assembly states to decompose manual pages into single-part operations and recover an assembly-tree. Then, it uses iterative after-state feedback refinement to guide successive (SE(3)) updates and corrections, and validates their physical plausibility through simulation-based release tests. Experiments show that compared with the strongest prior baseline, AssemState improves F1 from 38.58\% to 62.80\% and Tree Exact Match from 28.24\% to 53.92\% for assembly-tree recovery. On 243 independently evaluated part-level operations, our proposed iterative refinement improves judge-accepted operations from 0 to 5.3\% and reduces mean Chamfer distance from 5.4111 to 1.7744. However, visually plausible candidate poses may still suffer from collision, floating, mirror-orientation errors, incomplete seating, and wrong-side attachment. These results show that AssemState improves operation-structure recovery and selected local pose metrics, while MLLMs remain limited for spatial relationship reasoning.

authors.name: Zhiyuan Qi, Jierui Li, Yifan Shen, Cheng Qian, Jiateng Liu

papers.title: Self-Supervised Keyframe Discovery for Horizon-Invariant Behavior Cloning
papers.summary: Behavior cloning (BC) in non-Markovian environments is a challenging problem because policies have to reason over contextual information over long horizons. Existing policy architectures rely on recurrent or attention-based mechanisms to capture long-term dependencies. However, recurrent models suffer from hidden-state collapse and gradient instability under backpropagation through time while attention-based models are fundamentally limited by context length. To address these issues, we propose Keyframe Mnemonics, a novel self-supervised method that $\textit{discovers}$ a set of information-critical observations ($\textit{mnemonics}$) by learning an objective from randomly sampled past observations and using it as a reward for keyframe selection. We then train a BC policy that conditions on the discovered keyframes to model the action distribution. Under the simplicity bias assumption, our formulation provides context retention guarantees over an infinite horizon, while maintaining a small set of decision-relevant keyframes in the policy's working memory. We evaluate our method on synthetic memory domains, where mnemonic-conditioned BC policies achieve $100$% success rates (SR) and generalize to horizons orders of magnitude beyond training without performance degradation. Moreover, we evaluate on a memory-intensive robot manipulation benchmark, achieving a $13.9$% average absolute SR improvement over the strongest baseline across $23$ tasks. Finally, we demonstrate generalization with $80$% SR at $20\times$ longer time horizons on a real robot. Code and videos available at https://keyframe-mnemonics.github.io.

authors.name: Prabin Kumar Rath, Omkar Patil, Nakul Gopalan

papers.title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
papers.summary: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark that separates the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: natural-language scenarios describe the system, while a hidden causal model defines the data, the effect of every intervention, and the oracle answers. In ACED-Repair, agents diagnose a failing production system: within 15 experiments they must decide which controls to test, read confounded and filtered data, and recommend a fix, which we re-simulate on a hidden true objective. In ACED-Query, agents answer causal questions and make constrained causal decisions in worlds backed by categorical probabilistic graphical models. Acceptance on ACED-Repair ranges from 43% to 0% across 12 LLMs, while strong agents approach ceiling on ACED-Query's qualification questions. Tracing every experiment shows where investigations stop: most open-weight models test a true lever on its own in fewer than half of the worlds, the strongest models test the right levers but often miss the working dose or combination, and agents that do run a working fix almost always recommend it. No model reliably repairs systems with two independent causes or systems that need a subgroup-specific policy. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for choosing experiments, keeping track of evidence, and composing interventions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/ACED-Bench.

authors.name: Yiwei Chen, Amila Weerasinghe, Siddharth Biswal, Utkrisht Rajkumar, Olcay Boz, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Rose Yu

papers.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
papers.summary: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. It then projects that document into a runtime scaffold, machine-readable contracts, and deterministic tests. Eight specialized agents next carry out production: scenes are implemented serially, assets are produced in parallel, and one reduced manifest joins the two branches into a single build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. We evaluate finished games separately, through their rendered interfaces alone, over prompt-matched tasks run under a common protocol. GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline. In a side-by-side human study, raters also score GCA's games higher on every dimension and prefer them overall.

authors.name: Xiangxin Zhou, Jiaqi Tang, Ke Ma, Wenhao Yang, Jiarui Yao, Boye Niu, Haiyang Guo, Yifei Zhao, Huanjin Yao, Pu Jian, Ruihuang Li, Haitao Wu, Yushi Huang, Xiangyan Liu, Yan Sun, Kaixin Li, Tianyu Pang

papers.title: Sensitivity Analysis of Decision Rules in an Agent-Based Agro-Ecological Model
papers.summary: Agent-based models are well-suited for modelling agro-ecological systems for decision-making, yet turning their simulations into actionable insight requires identifying which decisions actually drive the behaviours. In such a context, sensitivity analysis stumbles upon a structural feature of many complex systems: the parameters are not a flat vector but a decision tree in which many parameters appear only when a higher-level choice activates them. Classical global sensitivity analysis presupposes independent inputs over a fixed Cartesian product and is ill-posed on such a branched space and biased by construction. We instead treat the structure of the decisions as a first-class modelling object. Using advanced surrogate modelling techniques, we encode the crop-management itinerary of the high-resolution agro-ecological modelling platform MAELIA as a hierarchical design space featuring both categorical and numerical variables. We propose a novel dedicated method to analyse this kind of hierarchical space, a random-forest-supervised HSIC-ANOVA, which ranks main effects and interactions natively on the tree while placing rarely and always active decisions on an equal footing. We show how, when applied to simulation outputs such as nitrogen leaching, soil organic carbon variation, and yield predictions, it can deliver an interpretable, decision-oriented reading.

authors.name: Benjamin Pianet, Baptiste Lesquoy, Paul Saves, Benoit Gaudou, Jean Villerd, Nicolas Verstaevel, Olivier Therond

papers.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
papers.summary: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.

authors.name: Dawei Li, Bohan Jiang, Huan Liu

papers.title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
papers.summary: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce LG-Bench, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

authors.name: Lu Sun, Xiangyi Zhang, Xiangyang Zhu, Zijian Chen, Qiang Hu, Yuan Tian, Guangtao Zhai

papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.summary: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.

authors.name: Jingwei Ni, Dmitry Abulkhanov, Vladislav Smirnov, Markus Leippold, Elliott Ash, Timothy Baldwin, Artem Shelmanov, Mrinmaya Sachan

papers.title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
papers.summary: Medical knowledge evolves, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate revisions into clinical recommendations remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change and 275 guideline lineages, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from its full incorporation. With updated guideline evidence explicitly provided, revision recognition exceeded full incorporation across 14 models, with a 20.1-percentage-point gap in the strongest model. For Qwen3-4B, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions, 80.2% were clinically correct, and 58.5% fully incorporated them, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point gap. Two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses yielded a 40.3-percentage-point gap in this enriched validation sample; 61 of 144 responses with incomplete incorporation were clinically incorrect. Prompting Qwen3-4B to prioritize revised evidence reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness without significantly improving full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of revised guidance as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability.

authors.name: Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu, Rui Zhang

papers.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents
papers.summary: Language agents carry information from past experience into future tasks whose demands may be unknown or change over time. Valuing this memory requires following the decision capability available in history, retained in storage and realized through use, together with the costs of recovery and revision. We develop a decision-theoretic account that connects these stages. Drawing on comparison of statistical experiments, information acquisition and the value of computation, we express original, retained and realized value in units of avoided task loss. Recovery and revision extend this account to attainable risk-cost profiles and preservation across uses. Unknown demand produces a family of value comparisons, while interactive feedback makes future work depend on the agent's actions. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples establish how information timing, access, computation and demand shape these comparisons; a pointer with zero mutual information about an answer can reduce the cost of exact recovery. Complete-split studies on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S and PersonaMem cover 3,075 questions and two readers. They show complementary value from saved state and recovered evidence, task-dependent performance orderings, and the role of reuse in amortizing construction costs. Multi-project workflows connect correction to preservation and validation costs. Together, the theory and studies support decisions about what to retain, which recovery options to preserve, and how to adapt memory as evidence and objectives evolve.

authors.name: Zehao Lin, Erenkai Zhu, Helan Hu, Xixuan Hao, Chunyu Li, Kai Chen, Feiyu Xiong

papers.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
papers.summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.

authors.name: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haicheng Liao, Yinhai Wang

papers.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
papers.summary: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 17 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy differential equation benchmarks, LegoSR Agent nearly matches the recovery coverage of seven expert-tuned methods combined and exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 29.4 percentage points, with 51-61% shorter median wall-clock time.

authors.name: Hao Mao, Xu T. Liu, Hao Xu, Peng Zhao, Qian Li, Dongxiao Zhang, Jinyue Yan, Yuntian Chen

papers.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
papers.summary: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

authors.name: Hoda Heidari, Aydin Mohseni

papers.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
papers.summary: Scaling supervised fine-tuning for working agents requires not only broad coverage of professional tasks, but also expert demonstrations that faithfully carry out professional workflows to completion. However, missing or inconsistent task information can disrupt expert demonstrations, weakening the resulting supervision. We introduce WorkFactory, a scalable task-construction framework that turns professional intents into executable task environments through hybrid intent sourcing, semantic workflow planning, and execution-based repair. Starting from these intents, WorkFactory constructs a Semantic Workflow Graph that explicitly represents information requirements, dependencies, and locations within the task environment. The graph guides the instantiation of task environments, while an adversarial execution-refinement loop exposes missing or inconsistent information and steers targeted repairs that preserve the original intent. Using WorkFactory, we construct 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and train the WorkPilot family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales on the resulting teacher trajectories. All three models improve over their respective base models across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B rising from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. Scaling experiments with up to 110k tasks further show that larger models benefit more from additional task data but exhibit diminishing returns at smaller data scales, while WorkPilot's long-horizon execution evolves from verbose trajectories toward more efficient task completion. Controlled component studies quantify the negative effects of task-environment defects on downstream performance and show how semantic workflow planning and execution-based repair yield downstream gains through improved task-environment quality. The subset of data are available at https://github.com/IQuestLab/WorkFactory.

authors.name: Ziyang Zeng, Tingyang Chen, Jia Deng, Qiyao Wang, Shuo Tang, Yike Yang, Tao Ren, Wayne Xin Zhao, Feng Chang, Jujie He, Chuan Hao, Ran Tao, Bryan Dai

papers.title: LiveSearch: Questions as Executable Verifier Code for a Live Benchmark of Professional-Source Financial Search Agents
papers.summary: In finance, the answer that matters is usually the current one: prices, rates, and disclosures hold only as of a given day, so retrieving up-to-date facts is a core capability of a financial agent. Yet most financial benchmarks overlook timeliness. They fix each answer at annotation time, so the gold goes stale as markets move and, once leaked into training data, rewards recall rather than search and analysis. We introduce LiveSearch, a live benchmark that stores each question as executable verifier code: a typed program of calls to a professional financial data service, followed by a declarative extractor. The question is frozen, while its gold answer is determined by executing the program against professional financial data at evaluation time, and a daily job re-executes it with no human or language model in the loop. A memorized answer is thus likely outdated, and a model must reach the current one through tools and analysis. Construction is equally automatic: a language model only verbalizes programs enumerated from real tool responses and never chooses an answer. Under general web search, six contemporary tool-calling models reach 70.9% to 76.7% answer accuracy. Over three consecutive days, 70% of served questions change their gold value, and even under tolerance-aware matching, a literally reused earlier snapshot fails on a majority of questions within a single day. Per-question tracking uncovers dynamic shifts in correctness masked by aggregate accuracy.

authors.name: Sinuo Wang, Wentao Zhao, Jiacheng Lu, Rui Sun, Beidi Luan, Qiming Shi, Jing Li, Daxin Jiang, Zuo Bai

papers.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
papers.summary: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

authors.name: Carole Lunny, Ian Goodman, Stefano Berrone, Connor TA Brenna, Emma K Reid, Ivan Perez-Neri, Shailesh Kolekar, Nityanand Jain, Ashwin Kamath, Lucas HCC Santos, Yulia Otmakhova, Heba Hussein, Diana M Cespedes, Gioia Dahdal, Salmaan Kanji

papers.title: P-ContextBench: From Personal Fact Recall to Personalized Agent Behavior
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for personal tasks, yet evaluating their safe use of personal context remains difficult because such contexts are private, fragmented, dynamic, and socially situated. We introduce P-ContextBench, a realistic, verifiable, and scalable benchmark for evaluating personal-context understanding. P-ContextBench constructs population-structured, life-story-grounded digital humans from demographic seeds reflecting the U.S. population. Rather than using explicit, static profiles, P-ContextBench embeds traits, routines, goals, and constraints as implicit evidence across fragmented, evolving synthetic mobile-app records. It evaluates five capabilities: single-source fact recovery, multi-source fact recovery, temporal state tracking, inference of higher-level personal patterns from routine behavior, and safe handling of requests conflicting with persona-specific constraints through compliance, warning, clarification, or refusal. A multi-stage validation pipeline checks persona plausibility, context recoverability, information leakage, evidence preservation, test-case grounding, and human-judge agreement. We instantiate P-ContextBench with 100 personas, 10,088 hidden facts, 18,261 app-trace fragments, and 4,810 verified test cases. The pipeline supports configurable generation across scales and demographic groups. Cost-effective state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs relevant to personal agents achieve below 60% accuracy on temporal tracking, higher-level pattern inference, and constraint-aware action-boundary decisions, with fewer than 10% of test cases answered correctly across all three repeated runs. Even a high-performing SOTA model remains inconsistent on these capabilities. P-ContextBench provides measurable targets for improving the accuracy, reliability, and safety of LLM-based personal agents.

authors.name: Grant Nasir Brown, Abdul Basir Bari, Anmol Tadikonda, Isabel Song

papers.title: Lifelong Learning of Scheduling Rules with Surrogate-assisted Genetic Programming for Dynamic Flexible Job Shop Scheduling
papers.summary: Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used to learn scheduling rules for dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS). However, trained rules tend to only generalise to tasks of similar scales and distributions, and when task characteristics change, learned rules often suffer significant performance degradation. Moreover, fine-tuning pre-trained rules on new tasks often leads to catastrophic forgetting, where prior knowledge is lost. This motivates the need for GP methods that can adapt to new tasks while preserving past knowledge, leading to a lifelong learning paradigm. However, lifelong learning in GP for DFJSS remains largely under-explored. To address this gap, this paper proposes a surrogate-assisted GP method for lifelong learning to handle sequential heterogeneous DFJSS tasks with job or batch arrivals. The framework includes three key components: an adaptive two-stage training strategy to balance plasticity and stability, a task-similarity-based weighting mechanism to regulate knowledge reuse, and an improved surrogate model with distance constraints to enhance estimation accuracy. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining strong adaptability, outperforming several compared methods and demonstrating the potential of lifelong GP in dynamic scheduling environments.

authors.name: Luyao Zhu, Fangfang Zhang, Yi Mei, Ke Chen, Mengjie Zhang

papers.title: Scaling Science: Toward a Chain Reaction of Discovery
papers.summary: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. Breaking this wall requires a paradigm shift in AI for Science: moving from passively mining questions out of existing datasets to actively generating and recombining experimental data around unresolved scientific questions. In a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates fresh evidence that stimulates further investigations. To enable these evidence-driven chain reactions, we propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint that connects shared scientific memory with distributed experimental loops. ESI preserves experimental records -- including negative and anomalous results -- in computable representations, allowing models to recombine evidence across domains into testable hypotheses. Rather than following fixed screening pipelines, the system jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, directing distributed laboratories to produce the exact evidence needed next. Their physical feedback revises both hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build this infrastructure for scaling science through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.

authors.name: Yuheng Ding

papers.title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
papers.summary: Large databases of paper-derived experimental materials data hide essential information on materials. Their analysis is demanding, large-scale and complex, making manual knowledge extraction very difficult. To address this challenge, we developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA) for automated, autonomous analysis of materials experimental big data and a specialized AI built on the obtained knowledge. MAA's nine role-specific AI agents, under predefined instructions and quality checks, autonomously perform data extraction, compositional feature generation, machine-learning modeling, feature-importance analysis and knowledge-base recording, iterating while inheriting previous knowledge. Delegating numerical processing to code makes large-scale data tractable; recording every choice and result enables later tracing to sources. In four thermoelectric-data experiments varying theme and cycle counts, the knowledge graph grew: knowledge clustered by theme and vocabulary was shared across themes. The specialized AI, searching and reading these records, answered materials questions citing sources. Retrospective verification also revealed errors, traced through the records to their sources.

authors.name: Yusuke Hashimoto, Takaaki Tomai

papers.title: CHATDIFY: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.summary: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

authors.name: Tao Fan, Guoqiang Ma

papers.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
papers.summary: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds together, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Reconstructed from real materials with 13 domain experts, its 11 projects span settings such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting. They comprise 150 subtasks, with 2-15 subsequent releases of new materials and client feedback per project. Later subtasks build on the agent's own earlier deliverables, so unresolved errors can carry into downstream work. Expert rubrics assess each subtask submission and the final delivery package. Across seven model-harness systems, the best scores 65.0/100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery; delivery also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

authors.name: Yumou Liu, Mingju Chen, Zhoufutu Wen, Qianyu Yang, Zijie Wang, Sihan Chen, Yeqian Liu, Chenghao Yang, Tiliang Duan, Qiyu Cai, Yanglihong Xiao, Jiayun Dong, Jianlan Ma, Shenhao Miao, Yuhan Cao, Lu Xu, Que Shen, Tian Gao, Ziyu Liang, Eric Yang, Ge Zhang, Jianpeng Jiao, Xuanhe Zhou, Fan Wu

papers.title: DiabAgent: Toward Agentic Physiological Control
papers.summary: As pretraining scales, medical language models have advanced rapidly in clinical question answering. Their ability to achieve effective physiological control through sustained intervention still lacks systematic quantitative evaluation. Type 1 diabetes provides a concrete setting: impaired insulin secretion creates dependence on exogenous insulin, with dosing continually adjusted using information about meals, exercise, illness, and glucose measurements. We introduce DiabAgent, a research suite for agentic physiological control comprising the Agentic Physiological Control (APC) framework, the DiabetSim simulator, and the SweetBench benchmark. APC controls glucose through medical-device tools, using ongoing observations to infer individual states, accumulate personal experience, and choose treatment actions. We build DiabetSim to simulate different patients, events, and device conditions for scalable virtual testing and training. Using DiabetSim, we construct SweetBench by instantiating 32 scenario designs as 212 glucose-control tasks. With Claude Opus 5.5 and a fixed decision interval of one hour, APC achieves a COGI of 73.5, compared with 71.2 for the open-source closed-loop baseline OpenAPS. Ablations further show that individual adaptation and contextual information improve glucose control. Combining high-frequency rule-based control with lower-frequency agent decisions shows potential for balancing control performance and computational cost. Our work provides a framework, simulator, and evaluation foundation for agents to participate in human physiological control.

authors.name: Chengxi Li, Shaoxuan Li, Deyao Hong, Qingle Liu, Yi Huang, Puheng Bian, Minzhi Xu, Lanyue Zhang, Mingze Sun, Xin Li, Calvin Xiao, Shengyuan Wang, Huan-ang Gao, Jiazheng Xu, Kaisen Yang, Hongning Wang

papers.title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
papers.summary: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

authors.name: Shuzheng Gao, Zhaojian Yu, Penghao Yin, Yuling Shi, Kai Cai, Shilin He, Michael R. Lyu

papers.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
papers.summary: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in a 136.3 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. In a matched fine-grid test, broadening the trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum by 1.80 ns and recovers an early 153 J bolometric deficit to within 0.08% by 44 ns, with a spectral response that shifts during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.

authors.name: Bowen Zhu, Jian Wu

papers.title: Embodied AI for Scientific Discovery: From Physical Action to Scientific Evidence
papers.summary: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.

authors.name: Wenhao Xu, Changwei Wang, Shunpeng Chen, Yukun Song, Sifan Zhou, Kaize Luo, Shibiao Xu, Yuehua Zhao, Rongtao Xu

papers.title: CogniLife: Continuous Cognitive Distillation for Deployed Multi-Expert Agent Marketplaces
papers.summary: Multi-expert agent marketplaces -- where creators publish domain-specific AI experts for end users to consult -- are an emerging deployment pattern for language technology. A published expert can receive many requests yet little evidence about its creator, who remains active elsewhere: the cold-expert problem. We frame continuous cognitive distillation as converting attributed creator observations into revisable decision rules, communication patterns, and domain procedures. CogniLife proposes a cross-expert attribution design for this problem, with Creator Profiles for transferable creator patterns and Expert Journals for listing-specific knowledge; this design is not yet implemented or evaluated. A deployed platform partially realizes the surrounding lifecycle through creator-authorized authoring, capability-owned proposal filtering, and reversible consolidation of eligible owner-scoped memory. On ProfyBench-v1, an 85-task offline benchmark built from replay seeds and controlled internal tests, the Profy Full configuration as a whole achieves a mean overall score of 4.65/5 from the primary LLM judge, compared with 4.01 for Raw LLM and 4.28 for Expert Prompt, with the largest gains in completeness, specificity, and missing-information tasks. These configuration-level scores do not test cold-expert mitigation, cross-expert transfer, or longitudinal distillation.

authors.name: Xuwei Tan, Jingchun Huang, Ming Cai, Shuangquan Lyu, Tiange Wang, Yinzhi Wang, Ronghua Shi, Jingwei Song, Yinghui Xia, Hehua Fan, Yifan Zhou, Hanxin Chen, Jiwei Song, Yang Jingsong, Tianyu Shi

papers.title: EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design
papers.summary: Enzyme engineering usually optimises which candidates to assay within a fixed model and workflow; when the bottleneck is a mismatched method or a failing workflow, that route is hard to escape. We present EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop system for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The outer loop evolves harness assets without changing model weights; the inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms under controlled conditions; a cloud laboratory system is specified for closing the physical loop with quality-controlled feedback. The outer loop raised the mean development-set Spearman correlation on ProteinGym by 0.044 across five assays, reaching 0.335 on CD19 and 0.683 on OPSD (rhodopsin); of the two first places, only CD19 was produced by the outer loop itself. In ThermoMPNN self-improvement the inner loop reached a PCC of 0.849, and on TadA-Bench a Spearman correlation of 0.307 in 1.13 h. We examined the system's experimental decision-making in three enzyme systems. For the luciferase RLuc, 10 of the 32 nominated substitutions not pre-specified reached at least twice wild-type activity in a single round. For the cytidine deaminase A3A, a variant selected by a rule that caps loss of unmodified C raised 5mC conversion in the weaker CT context from 11.4% to 46.5% and reversed the substrate preference in both contexts. For the DNA polymerase KOD-E, 189 single-substitution variants defined a landscape on which different objective functions selected divergent next steps from the same parent; one assayed combination reached 31.1 times the parent on a modified substrate. By treating the organisation of research and the development of algorithms as separately scored objects of evolution, and linking a frozen decision record to a physical measurement, this work offers an evolutionary paradigm for moving beyond the blind spots of a fixed method and for autonomous enzyme engineering.

authors.name: Genoria AI Team, Yuejie Hou, Lixiang Yang, Yisi Liu, Weiting Tang, Yueyuxiao Yang, Meng Yang

papers.title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
papers.summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

authors.name: Yichen Sun, Qirui Liu, Yan Wang, Jianan Lin, Linbo Jiang, Shiyu Wang, Zhibo Wang, Zhixuan Chu

papers.title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
papers.summary: AI agents are expanding from personal assistance into professional services delivered to external clients on an individual's behalf. We define a personal external service agent as one authorized and managed on an ongoing basis by an individual. It uses that person's knowledge, experience, and professional methods to accept client work, deliver results, and provide follow-up support. Client feedback, professional reputation, and potential income may give individuals more direct incentives to keep developing and improving agents for external services than for personal assistance. Yet building a safe, reliable external service system independently remains difficult, even with AI-assisted programming. People without AI expertise need platforms that are easy to use and safe to operate, with support for creating, developing, and running their agents. We propose the DelegateEval evaluation framework and experimental design to assess these platforms and guide their development. The framework covers eight dimensions: ease of creation and management, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. A complete dataset, executable environment, and unified scoring protocol remain to be developed, and empirical validation across foundation models has yet to be conducted.

authors.name: Jichao Li, Jinrong Lu, Manjiang Yu, Zhixuan Liu

papers.title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
papers.summary: Resource closures, arrival delays, and processing-time extensions jointly alter station operations during disruptions. Uncertain reopening times further complicate decisions about holding trains and selecting alternative routes. We use observations of disruption-resolution stages to update conditional predictions of the remaining closure duration. A distributionally robust model accounts for errors in scenario probability estimates and jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. Logic-based Benders decomposition coordinates routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts exploit resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the solution order of resource relaxations. Together, these components form the GNN-LBBD algorithm. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min.
