If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.

authors.name: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Youran Sun, Jingxin Yang, Kejia Zhang, Haizhao Yang

papers.title: Watching Itself Watch: Self-Auditing Visual Reliance for Video Reasoning
papers.summary: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: https://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/VIOS/

authors.name: Rohan Dugad, Mi Luo, Kristen Grauman

papers.title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization
papers.summary: Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold $\eta$, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate $(\eta-2\Gamma)_+$, with an exact early exit when $\eta\leq 2\Gamma$. Experiments on contextual fractional knapsack validate the geometry and certificates: continuous refinement reduces the $0.95$-quantile and $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.95}$ of regret by $9.1\%$ and $13.1\%$ relative to nominal PTO, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only $10.0\%$ of nominal decisions.

authors.name: Lingjie Zhao, Hansheng Jiang, Wei Qi

papers.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
papers.summary: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

authors.name: Wei Chen, Lihao Zhuang, Yubing Wu, Delu Zeng

papers.title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
papers.summary: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE.

authors.name: Donghyun Kim, Jin Hong, Seungmin Kim, Dain Kim, Junseok Kwon, Daeseon Choi

papers.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
papers.summary: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

authors.name: Moritz Poguntke, Eda Oktay, Yuanzhe Xi, Erin Carson, Martin Stoll

papers.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
papers.summary: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

authors.name: Tuo Liu, Edgar Dobriban, Francesco Orabona

papers.title: BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
papers.summary: We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.

authors.name: Taemin Cho, Hector Martel, Enyan Koh

papers.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
papers.summary: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.

authors.name: Adrian Johannes Staeves, Mayur Rattan Jaisinghani, Rebekah Overdorf, Frank Breitinger

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Non-Interactive Encrypted Neural Network Training with Batched Diagonal Packing
papers.summary: Training a neural network under homomorphic encryption requires transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates, and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products. We combine rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation, and compact optimizer state in an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation. Its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU, while retaining host key generation and client operations. In a matched 100-update experiment on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping reduces training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds, a $48.68\times$ ratio against our CPU implementation, with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions. Including setup and final evaluation gives a $40.67\times$ ratio. A separate GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds and achieves 90.35% test accuracy versus 90.41% for its plaintext twin. These are single-initialization results; exact CPU/GPU parameter agreement is verified at 100 updates, not for the full 1,000-update run. Earlier completed CPU runs support a larger-batch key-switch advantage and baseline-batch accuracy within the registered tolerance, but the baseline-batch normalized key-switch target is missed. The released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold, and its full-setting CPU time is unmeasured. We therefore distinguish measured acceleration of our implementation from conditional layout comparisons and do not claim unconditional superiority over ReBoot.

authors.name: Kentaro Mihara

papers.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
papers.summary: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

authors.name: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du, Minchen Li, Tuur Stuyck, Miles Macklin, Kui Wu, Bo Zhu, Yin Yang, Ming C. Lin, Alberta Longhini, Rika Antonova, Leonidas Guibas, Gordon Wetzstein, Jeannette Bohg, Chenfanfu Jiang

papers.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
papers.summary: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.

authors.name: Jiantong Xu

papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.

authors.name: Tomas Rasymas, Povilas Kvedaras

papers.title: CADMA: Capacity-Aware Coverage Decomposition for Generative Model Assessment
papers.summary: Evaluating generative models requires measuring not only sample fidelity but also how well a generated set covers the real data distribution. Recent work has therefore introduced recall-oriented metrics for distribution-level evaluation. However, existing recall metrics often reduce distributional coverage to geometry-based coverage. This simplifying assumption weakens their diagnostic value and interpretability in two ways: these metrics provide only a single aggregate score that cannot distinguish essential diversity failures such as mode dropping and mode collapse, and geometry-based coverage can provide unreliable estimates by assigning high scores to poorly covered generative distributions. We therefore introduce CADMA, a capacity-aware framework for recall-oriented evaluation and diagnosis. CADMA evaluates distributional coverage through local capacity matching between real and generated samples, separating geometry-based coverage from effective coverage. This yields multi-dimensional coverage diagnostics that quantify mode dropping and mode collapse while reducing the overly optimistic estimates produced by geometry-based metrics. Through extensive experiments on toy data, real-world datasets, and generative models, we show that CADMA provides more reliable coverage estimates and more fine-grained, interpretable diagnostic signals of diversity failures than existing metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Open-Debin/CADMA_NeurIPS2026.

authors.name: Debin Meng, Zheng Gao, Ziquan Liu, Yanran Li, Ioannis Patras, Georgios Tzimiropoulos

papers.title: Hierarchical Multi-Channel Tip-Over Prediction via Isolated Temporal Models for Planetary Rover Safety
papers.summary: Reliable tip-over prevention is critical for planetary rovers operating in unstructured environments where communication delays prevent real-time human intervention. Existing learning-based approaches typically optimize a single prediction objective, limiting their ability to capture both gradual instability evolution and abrupt terrain disturbances. This work presents a hierarchical multi-channel tip-over prediction framework based on isolated temporal learning. A multi-horizon Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) learns progressive instability patterns from inertial measurements, while a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based forward dynamics model predicts nominal rover motion and detects unexpected dynamic deviations through prediction residuals. These complementary signals are integrated through decision-level fusion and priority-based arbitration to generate graded safety actions, including early warning and emergency braking. The proposed system is deployed as an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT)-based safety component within the Rock robotics framework, operating at 100 Hz on a planetary rover software stack. Experiments on Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) samples collected across heterogeneous terrains demonstrate 97.58% event prediction coverage with a 1.82s median lead time, outperforming individual prediction channels. The results validate that isolated temporal models combined through hierarchical decision fusion provide a robust solution for real-time rover safety in uncertain terrain.

authors.name: Siddhant Shete, Raul Dominguez, Frank Kirchner

papers.title: Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks for Damage Identification in Ultrasonic Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
papers.summary: Ultrasonic guided wave (UGW) inspection has become an effective method in structural health monitoring (SHM). While machine learning has enhanced damage detection capabilities, purely data-driven models remain constrained by extensive labeled datasets and limited physical interpretability. Standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) further suffer from spectral bias (F-Principle) in high-frequency regimes, prioritizing low-frequency components while failing to resolve the high-frequency oscillations critical for UGW reconstruction. Physics-Informed Sinusoidal Representation Networks (PI-SIRENs) address these limitations by embedding governing partial differential equations directly into the training process. Building upon SIRENs, which utilize periodic activation functions to inherently capture high-frequency spectral content, the proposed framework is designed to operate effectively in sparse ultrasonic measurement regimes. This work introduces a frequency-domain PI-SIREN framework tailored for the Mindlin-Reissner plate theory to reconstruct ultrasonic wavefields without temporal discretization. The model parameters are optimized using a hybrid strategy comprising three phases: first-order Adam, residual-adaptive refinement (RAR) and quasi-Newton L-BFGS. Numerical and experimental evaluations confirm that the model serves as a physics-consistent baseline derived from sparse data, functioning as a computationally efficient surrogate for damage identification in SHM and non-destructive testing (NDT). Integrating the surrogate into a damage identification pipeline detects and localizes a milled notch from sparse experimental measurements with a localization error of 1 % of the plate diagonal. In contrast, data-driven benchmarks and MLPs with hyperbolic tangent activation functions, with and without Fourier feature embedding, are unable to identify damage due to higher reconstruction errors.

authors.name: Lukas Jilke, Caspar Wasle, Norbert Hosters, Florian Raddatz, Marek Behr, Gerko Wende

papers.title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

authors.name: Junha Ryu, Hoi-Jun Yoo

papers.title: Tensor Network Kernel Machines for Nonlinear System Identification
papers.summary: Over the past ten years Tensor Network Kernel Machines have enabled efficient nonlinear system identification through the use of low-rank tensor networks. The goal of this article is to provide the reader with a basic understanding of this model class in terms of its two defining properties. Furthermore, both the optimization and regularization of such models are discussed, together with recent developments and starting points for further exploration.

authors.name: Kim Batselier

papers.title: AudioCodex: Streaming Autoencoders for Live Audio
papers.summary: We introduce AudioCodex, a fully causal autoencoder for live generative audio applications that compresses stereo audio into compact continuous latent sequences at ~10 Hz. It combines a Mean Flow magnitude autoencoder with latent hypersphere projection, bounded-noise augmentation, representation alignment, and adversarial phase recovery to learn representations that support both efficient downstream generation and high-quality reconstruction. Through extensive ablations, we show that AudioCodex outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of generation-reconstruction trade-off, whilst remaining strictly causal in both encoding and decoding. This work paves the way towards truly real-time interactive and streaming generative audio applications.

authors.name: Marco Pasini, Javier Nistal, Cyran Aouameur, Stefan Lattner, George Fazekas

papers.title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
papers.summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

authors.name: Roger Guimer\`a, Kai-Hendrik Cohrs, Sergio Pedreira, Marta Sales-Pardo, Gustau Camps-Valls

papers.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
papers.summary: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

authors.name: Zhaohui Xu, Xiaofei Xu, Doudou Zhou

papers.title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
papers.summary: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

authors.name: Paul H\"ausner, Jevgenija Rudzusika, Jens Sj\"olund, Ozan \"Oktem

papers.title: Evaluating Cross-Signal Coherence in Mammography Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.

authors.name: Rebeca Nam, Chase M. Fensore, Christian A. Fauria-Robinson, Judy Gichoya, Joyce C. Ho

papers.title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
papers.summary: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.

authors.name: Zequan Liu

papers.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
papers.summary: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12\Delta^\top F\Delta$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $\alpha^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

authors.name: Dezhen Lu, Zixiang Ni

papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

authors.name: Mat\v{e}j Kripner, Milan Straka

papers.title: A four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: a body composition case study
papers.summary: Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET) lack prognostic biomarkers, and computed tomography (CT)-based body composition radiomics at the third lumbar vertebra (L3) is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations variable and optimistic. This methodological study proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: (1) false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected feature selection, (2) a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularization, (3) repeated nested cross-validation (CV) and (4) a negative control with Gaussian noise features. In 78 GEP-NET patients, 535 radiomic features from five L3 compartments were used to evaluate five survival models with Harrell's concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and integrated Brier score (IBS). Step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds under noise (nominal level 20%) versus 84% with radiomic features. The dual-path comparison showed no consistent difference between strategies. Repeated nested CV reduced variability across seeds (41% median reduction in C-index standard deviation), but not enough to distinguish models. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07-0.15 with radiomic features but not clearly under noise (0.40-0.42 with prior feature selection, 0.47-0.55 with embedded regularization). Frequently selected features tentatively linked greater subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle compactness and texture to better prognosis. These findings suggest a modest prognostic signal in L3 radiomics, with considerable uncertainty that the protocol quantifies. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies. Code: https://github.com/marielatalaveram/radiomics-survival-validation-protocol.

authors.name: Mariela Talavera-Mu\~noz, Cecilia Diana-Albelda, Miguel Antonio Sampedro-Nu\~nez, Victor Rodriguez-Laval, Jesus Bescos, \'Alvaro Garc\'ia-Mart\'in

papers.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
papers.summary: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.

authors.name: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi, Donald B. Rubin

papers.title: Hidden Tails: Certifying Tail-Risk Claims under Selective Labels
papers.summary: Historical decisions determine which outcomes are observed, potentially concealing a predictor's largest errors. Even unlimited data from the same observation process can therefore leave population tail risk unresolved. Here we derive sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk, the average loss in a specified upper tail, for binary outcomes and bounded losses. These bounds span exactly the risks compatible with the observations and a stated limit on how outcome odds differ between observed and hidden cases at the same covariate values. Under stated regularity conditions, calibrated statistical certificates cover these ranges simultaneously across candidate predictors, supporting risk limits and model comparisons while separating statistical uncertainty from persistent ambiguity. For a fixed predictor and loss threshold, we derive a minimum-cost allocation for reducing excess-loss ambiguity by prioritizing hidden outcomes according to ambiguity removed per unit cost. This allocation treats audited population contributions as known and retains the original sensitivity bounds separately for audited and still-hidden outcomes. In controlled masking experiments with known loan repayments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removes a median 61% of estimated fixed-threshold ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery. These results connect population tail-risk claims to the available evidence and identify where additional outcomes can sharpen their assessment.

authors.name: El Mustapha Mansouri

papers.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
papers.summary: Selecting an effective cover photo is a critical yet understudied problem in visual merchandising for e-commerce marketplaces. On Airbnb, hosts upload many photos depicting different rooms, amenities, and points of interest, but must manually choose a single static cover photo that is reused across heterogeneous product surfaces. This creates substantial challenges: over 90\% of listing photos have no engagement labels, leading to a severe cold-start regime; guest preferences vary across surfaces and search intents, and visually captivating photos may be semantically misaligned with the underlying listing. At Airbnb scale, this corresponds to hundreds of millions of photos and hundreds of thousands of new uploads per day. We propose \emph{OptiCover}, a scalable framework for cold-start visual optimization under semantic constraints and multi-surface engagement signals. The framework combines (i) a photo candidate generator that identifies candidate photos through various proxies, (ii) lightweight vision heads applied to frozen CLIP embeddings for large-scale semantic scoring, (iii) a cross-modal grounding validator based on a vision-language model (VLM) that enforces semantic representativeness, and (iv) an Exploration Logging Module (ELM) that orchestrates the collection of randomized engagement data across heterogeneous product surfaces and contextual search intents. We evaluate OptiCover through extensive offline studies and multiple online experiments across HomePage, and Search surfaces. OptiCover is now deployed in production and performs tens of millions of photo swaps daily. Online results show a 1.5\% engagement lift on the HomePage and a 0.35\% increase in bookers on Search, generating millions of dollars in incremental revenue. Our findings suggest that action-space shaping and semantic constraints are primary drivers of performance.

authors.name: Guillaume Guy, Mihajlo Grbovic, Joe Mills, Selen Uguroglu, Liwei He, Pratiksha Kadam, Nalini Kartha, Qian Aria Li

papers.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
papers.summary: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

authors.name: Dev Akre, Roman Bobalo, Manoj Dobbali

papers.title: From Granger causality to causal structure in dynamical systems
papers.summary: The idea of testing whether the past of one signal improves the prediction of another can be traced back to Wiener. It was Granger who formalized the concept. Granger causality has become one of the most widely used tools to infer directed interactions between the components of a system. The name however can be misleading: it detects predictive relations among the measured signals, not causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them. This article starts by reviewing recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis. It then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models, and asks under which conditions that structure can be read causally.

authors.name: V\'ictor Elvira

papers.title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
papers.summary: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincar\'{e} inequalities.

authors.name: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti

papers.title: What kills $v$-prediction? A Patch-wise PCA Perspective on Pixel-Space Flow Matching
papers.summary: Latent Diffusion Models dominate generative modeling but face two-stage training complexity and the inherent reconstruction limits of pre-trained autoencoders. Pixel-space Flow Matching offers a simplified end-to-end alternative yet often encounters training difficulties when using the standard $v$-prediction objective. Recent research attributes this difficulty to the off-manifold nature of noised targets, motivating a shift toward $x$-prediction. In this paper, we investigate this explanation through patch-wise Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and identify a bandwidth bottleneck. The velocity in minor components is largely determined by the raw noisy input, requiring deep backbones to preserve information that competes with principal-component modeling. Through controlled experiments and representation analysis, we further examine why $x$-prediction remains effective: its parameterization provides a raw-input bypass, while its learned input representation can spontaneously concentrate on principal directions. Under low-rank observations, our analysis of the induced flow characterizes $x$-prediction as an implicit conditional-mean decoder, reconstructing discarded components from the retained information. These observations motivate the Raw-injected Transformer (RiT), which combines a lightweight raw-conditioned decoder with an output-side shortcut to separate semantic modeling from raw-state propagation. Our method restores effective $v$-prediction and achieves competitive performance on ImageNet $256\times256$, providing a perspective on the interaction between prediction objectives and architectural bandwidth.

authors.name: Tianze Luo, Haofeng Huang, Yuan Yao

papers.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
papers.summary: Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in emergent misalignment. We discover a surprising "on-the-line" phenomenon in persona generalization: in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates across various fine-tuning hyperparameters follow an approximately probit-linear relationship, and the specific probit-linear relationship is surprisingly shared even across model families and model sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Training choices that leave the set of trainable parameters unchanged, such as learning rate, weight decay, and training duration, largely move models along the same line, reducing transfer mainly by weakening in-domain learning. Changing which layers are fine-tuned, however, can change the slope. For unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields shallower slopes, retaining strong in-domain learning while reducing out-of-domain misalignment. This "on-the-line" phenomenon unifies unexpected, isolated observations of persona generalization within a quantitative framework for predicting and controlling behavioral transfer.

authors.name: Olina Mukherjee, Arnav Goel, Aditi Raghunathan, Jacob Mitchell Springer

papers.title: TRAM: Test-Time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents
papers.summary: Deployed reinforcement learning agents often face safety requirements that are specified only after training: new hazard maps, revised risk thresholds, or behavioral alignment constraints. We study zero-update deployment-time adaptation in which a fixed library of risk-neutral source policies must be reused under a newly specified reward-risk tradeoff. We propose TRAM (Test-time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents), a source-scored composition rule that evaluates each source under the target reward and an occupancy-based deployment risk, then selects actions using risk-adjusted source scores. Unlike training-time risk-sensitive methods tied to a fixed surrogate such as return variance, TRAM supports spatial barrier exposure, divergence to a reference behavior, and local volatility risks specified at test time. We make the surrogate nature of the method explicit: TRAM is not claimed to solve the full occupancy-control problem of the stitched policy, but it admits a measurable source-hull mismatch term connecting source-scored risk to realized risk. Experiments in gridworlds, MuJoCo Reacher, Safety-Gymnasium, and an inference-time LLM alignment setting show that TRAM improves deployment risk while preserving reward and requires no parameter updates at test time.

authors.name: Mohamad Chehade, Amrit Singh Bedi, Souradip Chakraborty, Amy Zhang, Hao Zhu

papers.title: Neural Window Decoding of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes: Exploiting Window Structure for Learning and Adaptation
papers.summary: We propose a neural window decoder (NWD) for spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. The proposed methods adapt neural min-sum decoding to the structure and sequential operation of window decoding. First, target-oriented training restricts the loss to the variable nodes whose decisions are required at each window stage. Second, learned damping factors identify check-node updates that can reuse messages from the preceding iteration. Finally, adaptive weight switching selects weights trained for unreliable inherited information when a previous-window failure is detected. For a length-$20{,}000$ $(3,6)$-regular SC-LDPC code, the target-oriented NWD achieves performance comparable to sum-product window decoding while using min-sum updates. On the reduced target graph, scheduling based on regularized damping factors yields an estimated computational cost 48\% lower than that of full-graph weighted min-sum decoding, while maintaining comparable decoding performance. Adaptive weight switching improves decoding performance by 35\% at 3.0 dB relative to plain weights. These learning methods exploit the properties of window decoding to improve the reliability and computational efficiency of SC-LDPC convolutional codes.

authors.name: Dae-Young Yun, Hee-Youl Kwak, Sang-Hyo Kim, Yongjune Kim, Jong-Seon No

papers.title: Multi-Label Contrastive Learning : A Comprehensive Study
papers.summary: Multi-label classification, which involves assigning multiple labels to a single input, has emerged as a key area in both research and industry due to its wide-ranging applications. Designing effective loss functions is crucial for optimizing deep neural networks for this task, as they significantly influence model performance and efficiency. Traditional loss functions, which often maximize likelihood under the assumption of label independence, may struggle to capture complex label relationships. Recent research has turned to supervised contrastive learning, a method that aims to create a structured representation space by bringing similar instances closer together and pushing dissimilar ones apart. Although contrastive learning offers a promising approach, applying it to multi-label classification presents unique challenges, particularly in managing label interactions and data structure. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth study of contrastive learning loss for multi-label classification across diverse settings. These include datasets with both small and large numbers of labels, datasets with varying amounts of training data, and applications in both computer vision and natural language processing. Our empirical results indicate that the promising outcomes of contrastive learning are attributable not only to the consideration of label interactions but also to the robust optimization scheme of the contrastive loss. Furthermore, while the supervised contrastive loss function faces challenges with datasets containing a small number of labels and ranking-based metrics, it demonstrates excellent performance, particularly in terms of Macro-F1, on datasets with a large number of labels.

authors.name: Alexandre Audibert, Aur\'elien Gauffre, Massih-Reza Amini

papers.title: Accelerating AIGC Services with Latent Action Diffusion Scheduling in Edge Networks
papers.summary: Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has gained significant popularity for creating diverse content. However, current AIGC models primarily focus on content quality within a centralized framework, resulting in a high service delay and negative user experiences. The workload of an AIGC task is determined by model complexity and multi-layered encoder architectures, posing significant challenges for its modeling, deployment, and scheduling within resource-constrained edge networks. We model an offloading problem among edges for providing real AIGC services and propose \textbf{LAD-TS}, a novel Latent Action Diffusion-based Task Scheduling method that orchestrates multiple edge servers for expedited AIGC services by leveraging the diffusion model's conditional guidance capability and the reinforcement learning's environment interaction ability. We first design an innovative Latent Action Diffusion Network (LADN) model based on traditional diffusion models. We then incorporate the LADN model into deep reinforcement learning, forming an effective LAD-TS method for task scheduling in distributed edge networks. Meanwhile, we design a latent action diffusion strategy to achieve near-optimal decisions quickly by utilizing historical action probabilities instead of Gaussian noise. Furthermore, we implement a refined AIGC model and develop \textbf{DEdgeAI}, a prototype edge system with the refined AIGC model deployment to evaluate our LAD-TS method. DEdgeAI provides a real AIGC service for users, demonstrating up to $7.36\%-18.11\%$ and $34.07\%-94.96\%$ shorter service delays than the state-of-the-art methods and representative commercial platforms, respectively. We release our open-source code at https://github.com/ChangfuXu/DEdgeAI/

authors.name: Changfu Xu, Jianxiong Guo, Wanyu Lin, Haodong Zou, Yuzhu Liang, Xiaowen Chu, Jiannong Cao, Tian Wang

papers.title: Partially Decentralized Multi-Agent Q-Learning via Digital Cousins for Wireless Networks
papers.summary: Q-learning is a widely used reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for optimizing wireless networks, but faces challenges with large state-spaces. Recently proposed multi-environment mixed Q-learning (MEMQ) algorithm addresses these challenges by employing multiple Q-learning algorithms across multiple synthetically generated, distinct but structurally related environments, so-called digital cousins. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-agent MEMQ (M-MEMQ) for cooperative decentralized wireless networks with multiple networked transmitters (TXs) and base stations (BSs). TXs do not have access to global information (joint state and actions). The new concept of coordinated and uncoordinated states is introduced. In uncoordinated states, TXs act independently to minimize their individual costs and update local Q-functions. In coordinated states, TXs use a Bayesian approach to estimate the joint state and update the joint Q-functions. The cost of information-sharing scales linearly with the number of TXs and is independent of the joint state-action space size. Several theoretical guarantees, including deterministic and probabilistic convergence, bounds on estimation error variance, and the probability of misdetecting the joint states, are given. Numerical simulations show that M-MEMQ outperforms several decentralized and centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) multi-agent RL algorithms by achieving 60% lower average policy error (APE), 40% faster convergence, 45% reduced runtime complexity, and 40% less sample complexity. Furthermore, M-MEMQ achieves comparable APE with significantly lower complexity than centralized methods. Simulations validate the theoretical analyses.

authors.name: Talha Bozkus, Urbashi Mitra

papers.title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Spiking Neural Networks Trained by Local Learning
papers.summary: Recent research has shown the vulnerability of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) under adversarial examples that are nearly indistinguishable from clean data in the context of frame-based and event-based information. The majority of these studies are constrained in generating adversarial examples using Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT), a gradient-based method which lacks biological plausibility. In contrast, local learning methods, which relax many of BPTT's constraints, remain under-explored in the context of adversarial attacks. With the increasing real-world deployment of local learning methods in SNNs, it is critical to investigate whether these approaches introduce adversarial vulnerabilities that could compromise reliability. To address this problem, we examine adversarial robustness in SNNs through the framework of four types of training algorithms. We provide an in-depth analysis showing that direct gradient-based attacks are ineffective for locally trained models. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a hybrid adversarial attack paradigm that leverages the transferability of adversarial instances. The proposed hybrid approach demonstrates superior performance, outperforming existing adversarial attack methods. Furthermore, the generalizability of the method is assessed under multi-step adversarial attacks, adversarial attacks in black-box scenarios, and within the non-spiking domain.

authors.name: Jiaqi Lin, Abhronil Sengupta

papers.title: On the Depth of Monotone ReLU Neural Networks and ICNNs
papers.summary: We study two models of $\mathsf{ReLU}$ neural networks: monotone networks ($\mathsf{ReLU}^+$) and input convex neural networks ($\mathsf{ICNN}$). Our focus is on expressivity, mostly in terms of depth, and our motivation is to gain a better understanding of the depth required to exactly represent functions using neural networks with ReLU activations, a subject that has received a lot of attention lately. We prove several lower bounds on the depth required to represent functions by monotone ReLU networks and $\mathsf{ICNN}$. For the maximum function $\mathsf{MAX}_n$ computing the maximum of $n$ real numbers, we show that $\mathsf{ReLU}^+$ networks cannot compute $\mathsf{MAX}_n$, or even approximate it. We prove a sharp lower bound of $n-1$ on the $\mathsf{ICNN}$ depth complexity of $\mathsf{MAX}_n$. We also prove depth separations between $\mathsf{ReLU}$ networks and $\mathsf{ICNN}$s; for every $k$, there is a depth-$2$ $\mathsf{ReLU}$ network of size $O(k^2)$ that cannot be simulated by a depth-$k$ $\mathsf{ICNN}$. The proofs are based on deep connections between neural networks and polyhedral geometry, and also use isoperimetric properties of triangulations.

authors.name: Egor Bakaev, Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Daniel Reichman, Amir Yehudayoff

papers.title: Learning Reusable Behavioral Motifs for Continuous Animal Behavior Modeling
papers.summary: Natural behavior evolves continuously and often reuses movement structure across contexts, but existing behavioral segmentation methods typically assign a single discrete syllable at each time point or impose restrictive generative assumptions. We introduce Motif-based Continuous Dynamics (MCD), a computational framework that models behavior as time-varying combinations of reusable behavioral motifs. MCD learns motifs as latent behavior-level features from transition dynamics, through spectral representation learning within a reinforcement learning framework. MCD then infers policies that combine these motifs across time or context, through offline imitation learning. This formulation avoids hard behavioral boundaries while capturing continuity and compositionality. Across simulated gridworld and continuous-control tasks, mouse maze navigation and pose data, MCD identifies reusable motifs that explain task and temporal variation. MCD therefore provides a flexible and interpretable framework for computational behavior analysis. Code is available in https://github.com/G1NO3/MCD.

authors.name: Jiyi Wang, Jingyang Ke, Bo Dai, Anqi Wu

papers.title: LFM4Ads: Large Foundation Model for Ads Recommendation
papers.summary: Recent work leverages large-scale pretrained foundation models (FMs) to transfer generalizable representations to downstream advertising tasks. Most existing approaches transfer user representations (URs) and item representations (IRs), while underutilizing the user-item cross representations (CRs) generated by deeper interaction layers. Although a recent work transfers target-aware embeddings (TAEs), it requires real-time upstream FM inference alongside the downstream, introducing additional engineering complexity and overhead. To address these limitations, we propose Large Foundation Model for Ads Recommendation (LFM4Ads), an efficient pretrain-then-transfer paradigm for cross-domain ad recommendation. LFM4Ads jointly exploits URs, IRs, and CRs from the upstream FM. It extracts sample-level CRs from pretrained interaction layers and aggregates them into user-level CRs using a time-aware exponential moving average, thereby decoupling upstream inference from downstream online serving. To use CRs efficiently, we propose three downstream usages at different levels of granularity: feature-level gating to fuse CRs into downstream embeddings, module-level fine-tuning to yield downstream CRs, and model-level retrieval by matching CRs with IRs. LFM4Ads has been deployed on Tencent's advertising platform since Q4 2024. It has supported 10+ launches across major scenarios, yielding a platform-wide gross merchandise value (GMV) lift of 2.45% and annual revenue gains in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Offline experiments on KuaiRand-1K further demonstrate our effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhuangQu/LFM4Ads.

authors.name: Jie Jiang, Shangyu Zhang, Shijie Quan, Zhongren Wang, Tianqu Zhuang, Junwei Pan, Bo Fu, Yilong Sun, Jieying Lin, Jushuo Chen, Xiaotian Li, Wenjie Li, Zhixiang Feng, Xian Hu, Huiting Deng, Hua Lu, Jinpeng Wang, Boqi Dai, Xiaoyu Chen, Bin Hu, Lili Huang, Yanwen Wu, Yeshou Cai, Qi Zhou, Huang Tang, Chunfeng Yang, Chengguo Yin, Tingyu Jiang, Lifeng Wang, Shudong Huang, Dapeng Liu, Yuekui Yang, Shu-Tao Xia, Lei Xiao, Haijie Gu

papers.title: Statistical Complexity of Soft Bellman Residual Minimization
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning and offline inverse reinforcement learning aim to recover near-optimal value functions or reward models from a fixed batch of logged trajectories, yet current practice still struggles to enforce Bellman consistency scalably. Bellman residual minimization (BRM) has emerged as an attractive remedy. While globally convergent gradient-based soft (i.e., entropy-regularized) BRM methods for neural networks have recently been established, their statistical complexity under stochastic gradient descent remains largely unknown. In this paper, we address this theoretical gap for soft BRM. Through a Lyapunov-based analysis under a uniform PL condition in the auxiliary variable, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ primal argument stability bound up to optimization error and an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ statistical complexity for the soft BRM objective under the stated sampling conditions.

authors.name: Enoch H. Kang, Kyoungseok Jang

papers.title: Challenges in Non-Polymeric Crystal Structure Prediction: Why a Geometric, Permutation-Invariant Loss is Needed
papers.summary: Crystalline structure prediction is an essential prerequisite for designing materials with targeted properties. Yet, it is still an open challenge in materials design and drug discovery. Despite recent advances in computational materials science, accurately predicting three-dimensional non-polymeric crystal structures remains elusive. In this work, we focus on the molecular assembly problem, where a set~$\mathcal{S}$ of identical rigid molecules is packed to form a crystalline structure. Such a simplified formulation provides a useful approximation to the actual problem. However, while recent state-of-the-art methods have increasingly adopted sophisticated techniques, the underlying learning objective remains ill-posed. We propose a better formulation that introduces a loss function capturing key geometric molecular properties while ensuring permutation invariance over $\mathcal{S}$. Remarkably, we demonstrate that within this framework, a simple regression model already outperforms prior approaches, including flow matching techniques, on the COD-Cluster17 benchmark, a curated non-polymeric subset of the Crystallography Open Database (COD). Our code is available at https://github.com/inria-thoth/SinkFast.

authors.name: Emmanuel Jehanno, Romain Menegaux, Julien Mairal, Sergei Grudinin

papers.title: Staying in the Sweet Spot: Boost Reasoning Evolution via Responsive Rollout Difficulty Manipulation
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has advanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLVR methods often suffer from exploration inefficiency due to mismatches between problem difficulty and model capability: overly difficult problems hinder reasoning path discovery, while overly simple problems offer little learning signal. To address this, we first formalize the effect of problem difficulty by quantifying the relationship between loss descent magnitude and rollout accuracy. Building on this analysis, we propose SEELE, a supervision-aided RLVR framework that dynamically adjusts problem difficulty to lie within the high-performance region. SEELE augments each training sample by appending a hint (part of a full solution) for difficulty reduction. Unlike previous hint-based approaches, SEELE deliberately computes the hint length for each individual problem to achieve an optimal difficulty. The optimal hint length is determined via multi-round rollout sampling, where an item response theory model fits accuracy-hint pairs from previous rounds to predict the next-round hint. This instance-level, real-time difficulty adjustment aligns problem difficulty with the evolving model capability, thereby improving exploration efficiency. Experiments show that SEELE outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) by +10.0 and +8.4 points, respectively, and exceeds the best prior supervision-aided approach by +3.8 points on average across six math reasoning benchmarks.

authors.name: Ziheng Li, Zexu Sun, Jinman Zhao, Erxue Min, Yongcheng Zeng, Hui Wu, Hengyi Cai, Shuaiqiang Wang, Dawei Yin, Xu Chen, Zhi-Hong Deng

papers.title: Implicit Credit Learning for Sparse-Reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: When a cooperative team receives feedback only at the end of an episode, a single outcome must guide many agents' earlier actions. Learning a dense team reward helps, but its decomposition does not automatically give each agent a useful policy update. We introduce IMAP, an online method that fits a shared Q/V reward model by comparing completed episodes according to their observed terminal outcomes. Local Q/V residuals provide agent-specific rewards; the same normalized weights combine them for a centralized critic and scale local advantages for decentralized PPO actors. We characterize when these local updates follow the learned team objective. With full returns and frozen reward heads, a sharp bound relates their gradient error to variation in future Q/V compatibility; an exact identity identifies additional continuation terms for general GAE. In experiments with terminal-only feedback, IMAP's local-actor configuration attains the highest reported mean among the compared methods on all nine SMACv2 scenarios and four MAMuJoCo tasks, and on two of three SMACLite scenarios. Controlled relay interventions confirm the predicted changes in actor credit while holding the learned team reward fixed. The gradient result concerns the fitted objective; benchmark returns measure performance on the original task outcomes.

authors.name: The Viet Bui, Tien Mai, Hong Thanh Nguyen

papers.title: Machine learning approaches to seismic event classification in the Ostrava region
papers.summary: The north-eastern part of the Czech Republic, including the Czech part of the Upper Silesian Coal Basin, is among the most seismically active areas of the country. The seismic stations in the region record mining-induced events, which continue after the cessation of mining, natural earthquakes, which are rare but may originate in the same area, and quarry blasts. A rapid and reliable distinction between the three types is required for the routine evaluation of the continuously recorded data. We study their automatic discrimination with neural networks from short three-component windows starting one second before the P-wave onset. The main data set is the archive of the Seismic Polygon Fren\v{s}t\'{a}t (1992--2002), a triggered network whose records were recovered from the original format, cleaned with deterministic and learned quality checks and completed with automatically picked P-wave arrivals; it contains about 40,000 records of all three event types. Among five compared architectures, convolutional networks operating on short-time spectrograms outperform recurrent networks operating on magnitude spectra or on the raw waveform. The best model, EfficientNet-B0 applied to 24-s windows, reaches a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.96, and blasts and natural earthquakes are practically never confused with each other; class weighting and undersampling, the usual remedies for the strong class imbalance, lower the score. Finally, we examine the transfer to the station OKC, which monitors the region today with different instruments. A model trained on the archive alone fails on the modern records, whereas a single model trained on both data sets reaches a macro-F1 score of 0.96 on the archive and 0.92 on the modern station, where the accuracy is limited by the small number of catalogued natural earthquakes rather than by the model.

authors.name: Michael Skotnica, Marek Pecha, Jana Ru\v{s}ajov\'a, Bohdan Rieznikov, V\'it Wandrol, Mark\'eta R\"osnerov\'a, Jarom\'ir Knejzl\'ik

papers.title: WirelessMathBench-XL: An Auditable Benchmark for Wireless Mathematical Reasoning
papers.summary: Benchmarks built from arXiv papers can overlap the arXiv text used in LLM pretraining, yet technical-domain releases rarely ship the per-item evidence needed to check this. We introduce a reverse-probe n-gram audit that indexes the benchmark side and streams the corpus past it, so memory scales with the benchmark rather than the corpus and flags on the distributed problems can be inspected and recomputed. We instantiate it in WirelessMathBench-XL, a 4,027-problem benchmark for wireless mathematical reasoning built from 836 arXiv papers across 20 subfields, with multiple-choice, progressive fill-in, and full-equation-completion formats. Streaming 12.9 B RedPajama-arXiv 13-grams yields a strict zero-hit view $\mathcal{S}_0$ covering 95.7% of the problems, and shows that the Dolma and ProofPile-2 arXiv slices repackage the same RedPajama dump.
